items.text: Resolution of the dispute
items.text_en: Resolution of the dispute

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves the dispute by attributing to Rabbi Yehuda the view that a minor who understands the significance of the donation can be vowed for, and to Rabbi Nehemya the view that the minor must reach physical maturity (הבאת שתי שערות, growing two pubic hairs).

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael regarding the use of leftover funds: Rabbi Akiva holds they are used for future offerings, while Rabbi Yishmael holds they are used for the current year's needs.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva states that leftover shekel funds (מותר שקלים) are used for future communal offerings.
Rabbi Yishmael counters that leftover funds (מותר תרומה) are used for the current year's needs, not future ones.
The Gemara explains the reasoning behind Rabbi Akiva's position: leftover funds from one sacred purpose cannot be diverted (אין משנין מקדושה לקדושה) to another sacred purpose.

The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Akiva derives his position from a verse that indicates the funds are designated for the following year.
An alternative version of the discussion is introduced, questioning the reasoning of the opposing view.

The Gemara resolves that the nazirite's leftover funds are treated like communal shekalim (שקלים), which are designated for voluntary offerings without a specific declaration.

items.text: First answer: Distinction between Temple and city
items.text_en: First answer: Distinction between Temple and city

items.text: Objection: Coins found between locations

items.text: Second answer: Proximity and uncertainty
items.text_en: Second answer: Proximity and uncertainty
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides a second answer, explaining that in cases of uncertainty, we follow the majority of the location where the coin is found, and if it is equidistant, we rule stringently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a second answer: in cases of uncertainty about the location of a found coin, we follow the majority of the place where it was discovered.
The Gemara resolves that if the coin is found equidistant between two locations, we rule stringently (לחומרא).

items.text: Objection and resolution: Coins found near the treasury
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: Coins found near the treasury
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if coins are found very close to the treasury, they might still be consecrated. It resolves that the Mishnah's ruling applies only to coins found at a distance where they are presumed to be from the marketplace.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmiyah objects that coins found near the treasury might have fallen from the treasury itself and thus be consecrated.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's leniency applies only where guards are not commonly stationed, so coins found there are presumed to be from the marketplace.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: leftover coins and their status
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: leftover coins and their status
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that coins set aside for the half-shekel donation that are left over after the Temple treasury has been collected are not consecrated and may be used for other purposes. This establishes the baseline rule for the daf's discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that leftover coins set aside for the half-shekel donation are not consecrated and do not carry מעילה (misappropriation liability).

items.text: Gemara's first question: why no consecration?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: why no consecration?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the leftover coins are not consecrated, given that they were designated for a sacred purpose. It suggests that perhaps the designation itself should render them sacred, but the Mishnah rules otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the leftover coins are not consecrated, given that they were designated for a sacred purpose.

items.text: First answer: designation without action
items.text_en: First answer: designation without action
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that mere verbal designation does not consecrate the coins; only actual transfer to the Temple treasury does. Since the coins were never handed over, they remain unconsecrated.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers that mere verbal designation does not consecrate the coins; only actual transfer to the Temple treasury does, so since the coins were never handed over, they remain unconsecrated.

items.text: Objection and resolution: the case of a lost purse
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: the case of a lost purse
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a case where a purse of coins for the half-shekel is lost and then found; the Gemara resolves that the ruling depends on whether the coins were already mixed with the Temple treasury. This clarifies the limits of the first answer.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba raises an objection from a baraita about a lost purse of half-shekel coins, implying that the finder may keep the coins even if found after the collection period.
The Gemara rejects the objection by distinguishing that the coins had not yet been mixed with the Temple treasury (לא קדשי), so they are not consecrated and may be kept by the finder.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Collection of half-shekels
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Collection of half-shekels
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the half-shekel is collected annually from all Israelites for the Temple offerings, and any surplus from one year is used for the next year's communal offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that on the first of Adar, announcements are made about the half-shekel collection, and the surplus from the previous year's collection is used for the current year's communal offerings.

items.text: Gemara's question on surplus usage
items.text_en: Gemara's question on surplus usage
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether surplus funds from the half-shekel collection can be used for other Temple needs or only for the next year's offerings, citing a baraita that discusses the matter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita that discusses the use of surplus half-shekel funds, citing Rabbi Yishmael's opinion.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva argues that surplus funds are designated for the next year's offerings, while Rabbi Yishmael holds they can be used for any Temple need. The Gemara analyzes their positions.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva states that surplus shekel funds (מותר השקלים) are designated for the next year's offerings.
Rabbi Yishmael counters that surplus shekel funds may be used for any Temple need.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind each sage's position.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva views surplus as dedicated to the next year's communal offerings, which is a greater sanctity, while Rabbi Yishmael permits any Temple use.

items.text: Supporting baraita and conclusion
items.text_en: Supporting baraita and conclusion
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Akiva's view that surplus is for the next year, and the Gemara concludes that the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva due to the majority of sages agreeing with him.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Akiva's view that the surplus of shekel funds is designated for the next year.
The Gemara concludes that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Akiva, because the majority of sages agree with his position.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Surplus shekel funds
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Surplus shekel funds
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that leftover money from the shekel collection of one year is used for the next year's communal offerings. It also discusses the case where funds were designated for a specific purpose but not used.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that surplus funds from the shekel collection (תרומת הלשכה) are carried over for the communal offerings of the following year.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Source for the rule
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Source for the rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source or reasoning behind using surplus funds for the next year. It explores possible derivations from verses about the shekel collection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a question asking for the scriptural source or reasoning for the mishnah's rule about using surplus shekel funds for the next year.
The Gemara begins to answer by citing a verse, suggesting a possible derivation from Scripture.

items.text: First answer: From the verse about the shekel
items.text_en: First answer: From the verse about the shekel
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers by citing a verse that implies the shekel collection is for the service of the Tent of Meeting, and the surplus is for future needs. This is supported by a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers by citing a verse that implies the shekel collection is for the service of the Tent of Meeting, and the surplus is for future needs.
A baraita is cited to support the answer, confirming that the surplus is designated for future needs.

items.text: Objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: An objection is raised: the verse might only apply to the original collection, not surplus. The Gemara then offers an alternative explanation based on the principle of 'sanctity carries over'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the previous explanation might only apply to the original collection, not to surplus funds.
The Gemara offers an alternative explanation based on the principle that the sanctity of the original collection carries over to the surplus.

items.text: Discussion of designated funds
items.text_en: Discussion of designated funds
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines a case where funds were set aside for a specific offering but not used. It concludes that such funds are also carried over, based on a similar logic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether funds designated for a specific offering but not used are also carried over to the next year, based on the same logic as the Mishnah's rule.
The Gemara provides an answer that such designated funds are indeed carried over, citing a supporting reasoning.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Lost or stolen coins
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Lost or stolen coins
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where someone sets aside coins for his half-shekel and they are lost or stolen. If the treasurer has not yet collected the tax, the person must replace the coins; if the treasurer has already collected, the person is exempt. The Mishnah also discusses the case of a partner who designated coins for the tax and they were stolen.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of someone who set aside coins for his half-shekel and they were lost or stolen, ruling that if the treasurer has not yet collected, the person must replace them.
The Mishnah concludes that if the treasurer has already collected the tax, the person is exempt from replacing the coins.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's distinction between before and after the treasurer's collection. It asks why the status of the coins should change based on the treasurer's collection, since the person's obligation to give the half-shekel is independent of the coins' fate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's ruling about coins changing status after the treasurer's collection is necessary, since the obligation to give the half-shekel is independent of the coins' fate.

items.text: First answer: The coins are a loan to the Temple
items.text_en: First answer: The coins are a loan to the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches that once the treasurer has collected the tax, the coins are considered as if they were given as a loan to the Temple treasury. Therefore, if they are lost or stolen, the person is not liable to replace them because the Temple is responsible for the loan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches that once the treasurer has collected the tax, the coins are considered as if they were given as a loan (מלוה) to the Temple treasury, so the person is not liable to replace them if lost or stolen.

items.text: Objection and second answer: The coins are designated for the Temple
items.text_en: Objection and second answer: The coins are designated for the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the first answer implies the coins become Temple property immediately, which is not the case. It then offers a second answer: the Mishnah's ruling is based on the principle that once the treasurer has collected, the coins are considered designated for the Temple, and the person's obligation is fulfilled by the designation, so he does not need to replace them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the first answer is problematic because it implies the coins become Temple property immediately, which is not the case.

Rava offers a second answer: the Mishnah's ruling is based on the principle that once the treasurer has collected, the coins are considered designated for the Temple, and the person's obligation is fulfilled by the designation, so he does not need to replace them.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Lost or stolen coins
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Lost or stolen coins
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where someone sets aside coins for his half-shekel and they are lost or stolen. If he then designates other coins and the original ones are found, both sets go to the Temple treasury, and he is credited for only one donation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of someone who sets aside coins for his half-shekel and they are lost or stolen.
The Mishnah states that if he designates other coins and the original ones are found, both sets go to the Temple treasury.
The Mishnah concludes that both sets go to the Temple treasury, and he is credited for only one donation.

items.text: Gemara's question: Does the original owner still owe?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Does the original owner still owe?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the original owner is still liable for the half-shekel if the coins were stolen before reaching the Temple treasury. It explores the principle that once coins are designated for the Temple, the owner's obligation may be fulfilled even if the coins are lost.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if the half-shekel coins were stolen before reaching the Temple treasury, is the original owner still liable to pay, or is he exempt?

items.text: First answer: Based on a baraita
items.text_en: First answer: Based on a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the question by citing a baraita about a similar case with animal offerings. The baraita suggests that if the designated animal is lost and another is substituted, the original owner is not liable for the first animal, implying the same for coins.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a lost designated animal and a substitute, concluding the original owner is not liable for the first animal, to resolve the question about coins.

items.text: Objection: Distinction between animal and coins
items.text_en: Objection: Distinction between animal and coins
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita deals with an animal offering, where the animal itself is consecrated, whereas coins are merely a means of payment. Therefore, the case may not be analogous, and the question remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita deals with an animal offering, where the animal itself is consecrated, whereas coins are merely a means of payment, so the case may not be analogous.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The requirement for full-weight shekels
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The requirement for full-weight shekels
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that silver shekels donated to the Temple must be of full weight, and that underweight or damaged coins are not acceptable. It also discusses the process of exchanging such coins for proper ones.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the shekels donated to the Temple must be of full-weight silver, and that one may not reduce their weight.

items.text: Gemara's question: What is the source for this requirement?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: What is the source for this requirement?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source that mandates the shekels be of full weight. It cites a verse from Exodus and explains that the phrase 'half a shekel of the holy shekel' implies a standard weight.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source that mandates the shekels be of full weight.
The Gemara cites the verse 'מחצית השקל' (half a shekel of the holy shekel) to show that the shekel must be of the full standard weight.

items.text: Discussion: The weight of the shekel and its subdivisions
items.text_en: Discussion: The weight of the shekel and its subdivisions
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on the weight of the holy shekel, explaining that it is equivalent to a certain number of silver coins. It also discusses the possibility of using coins that are slightly underweight if they are still within an acceptable range.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by asking what the weight of the holy shekel is, and answers that it is equivalent to a certain number of silver coins (מעשר סלעים).
The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan's statement that the shekel's weight is fixed and one may not reduce it below the standard.

items.text: Objection: Can damaged coins be used?
items.text_en: Objection: Can damaged coins be used?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: if a coin is damaged or clipped, can it still be used for the half-shekel? It cites a baraita that distinguishes between coins that are merely worn and those that are actually broken.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a damaged or clipped coin (פגום) can be used for the half-shekel.
A baraita is cited that distinguishes between worn coins (שחופין) which are accepted and damaged coins (פגומין) which are not accepted.

items.text: Resolution: The distinction between worn and damaged coins
items.text_en: Resolution: The distinction between worn and damaged coins
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that worn coins are acceptable if they still retain most of their weight, while damaged or clipped coins are not. It also discusses the role of the Temple treasury in exchanging such coins.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing between worn coins (which are acceptable if they retain most of their weight) and damaged or clipped coins (which are not).
A baraita is cited to support the resolution, stating that worn coins are accepted from the public for the Temple treasury.
The Gemara explains the rationale: the Temple treasury exchanges worn coins for fresh ones, so they accept them from the public.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Lost or mixed shekel coins
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Lost or mixed shekel coins
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where coins designated for the shekel were lost or mixed with other coins, and rules that the original obligation remains until the coins are actually delivered to the Temple treasury.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that one who sets aside a shekel coin but loses it remains liable until the coin reaches the Temple treasury.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's implication that one is liable for the coins until they reach the treasury, asking whether this applies even if the coins were lost after being handed to the Temple officials.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's implication that one is liable for the coins until they reach the treasury, asking whether this applies even if the coins were lost after being handed to the Temple officials.

items.text: First answer: Liability until delivery to the treasury
items.text_en: First answer: Liability until delivery to the treasury
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the obligation continues until the coins are actually delivered to the Temple treasury, not merely set aside.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers that the obligation to give the half-shekel continues until the coins reach the Temple treasurer.

items.text: Objection and second answer: Distinction between lost and stolen
items.text_en: Objection and second answer: Distinction between lost and stolen
items.desc_en: An objection is raised based on a baraita, and the Gemara resolves it by distinguishing between coins that were lost (where liability continues) and coins that were stolen (where liability ends if the owner was not negligent).

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita: one who sets aside his shekel and it is lost is liable for its replacement.
The Gemara answers: there, the case is where the coin was lost (so the owner remains liable), here, the case is where it was stolen (so the owner is exempt if not negligent).
The Gemara concludes that in the case of theft, the owner is not liable for the coin's replacement.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Status of leftover funds
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Status of leftover funds
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that leftover funds from the Temple treasury (שירי הלשכה) are used for various communal needs. It introduces a dispute about whether these funds retain their consecrated status or become unconsecrated.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking what was done with the leftover funds from the Temple treasury (שירי הלשכה).
The Mishnah continues by stating that the leftover funds (מותר הלשכה) were used for communal needs, implying they retain their consecrated status.
Rabbi Yehuda offers a dissenting opinion about the status of the leftover funds, asserting that the מותר (surplus) is permitted for non-sacred use.

items.text: Gemara's question: Are leftovers consecrated?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Are leftovers consecrated?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the underlying principle: do the leftover funds remain consecrated (קודש) or become unconsecrated (חולין)? It cites a baraita to clarify the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita about leftover funds (שירי הלשכה) and asks whether they remain consecrated or become unconsecrated.
The baraita cites the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda holds the leftovers are קודש (consecrated), while the Sages hold they are חולין (unconsecrated).
The Gemara explains the reasoning: Rabbi Yehuda derives from a verse that leftovers are consecrated, while the Sages derive they are unconsecrated.

items.text: Analysis of the dispute's reasoning
items.text_en: Analysis of the dispute's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the reasoning behind each opinion. Rabbi Yehuda holds that the funds are consecrated because they were originally designated for Temple use, while the Sages consider them unconsecrated once the original purpose is fulfilled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning behind Rabbi Yehuda's position.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda holds that the funds remain consecrated because they were originally designated for Temple use.
The Gemara explains that the Sages hold that the funds are not considered consecrated once the original purpose is fulfilled.

items.text: Practical application: Use of leftover funds
items.text_en: Practical application: Use of leftover funds
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses how the leftover funds are actually used according to each opinion. Rabbi Yehuda permits their use for communal needs like city walls, while the Sages restrict them to Temple-related expenses.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabbi Yehuda permits using leftover funds for communal needs.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that the Sages forbid using leftover funds for communal needs, restricting them to Temple expenses.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The leftover funds and their use
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The leftover funds and their use
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that leftover shekel funds (שירי הלשכה) are used for the purchase of communal offerings (קרבנות ציבור). It specifies that these funds are not considered consecrated (הקדש) for any other purpose.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking what is done with the leftover shekel funds (שירי הלשכה) and answers that they are used to purchase communal burnt offerings (עולות ציבור).

items.text: Gemara's first question: Are the funds consecrated?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Are the funds consecrated?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the leftover funds are considered consecrated (הקדש) or unconsecrated (חולין). It raises the possibility that they might be treated as unconsecrated funds that are designated for a specific purpose.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the leftover funds are considered consecrated (הקדש) or unconsecrated (חולין). It raises the possibility that they might be treated as unconsecrated funds that are designated for a specific purpose.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion: The funds are unconsecrated
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion: The funds are unconsecrated
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda argues that the leftover funds are unconsecrated (חולין) and can be used for any purpose, including the purchase of communal offerings. He bases this on the principle that funds not explicitly designated for the Temple treasury are not consecrated.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that the leftover funds are unconsecrated (חולין) and therefore not subject to the law of מעילה (misuse of consecrated property).

items.text: The Sages' opinion: The funds are consecrated
items.text_en: The Sages' opinion: The funds are consecrated
items.desc_en: The Sages disagree with Rabbi Yehuda and hold that the leftover funds are consecrated (הקדש) and subject to the laws of מעילה (misuse of consecrated property). They argue that any funds collected for the Temple treasury retain their consecrated status unless explicitly redeemed.

sub.text: Stam's framing of the Sages' position
sub.text_en: Stam's framing of the Sages' position
sub.desc_en: The Sages state that the leftover funds are consecrated (קודש), establishing the premise of their disagreement with Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.text: Stam's explanation of the Sages' reasoning
sub.text_en: Stam's explanation of the Sages' reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Sages conclude that the leftover funds retain consecrated status and therefore are subject to the laws of מעילה (misuse of consecrated property), reinforcing their legal stance.

items.text: Gemara's resolution: The practical difference
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution: The practical difference
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the practical difference between the two opinions is whether the funds can be used for the purchase of communal offerings without additional consecration. According to Rabbi Yehuda, they can be used directly, while according to the Sages, they must first be consecrated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between the two opinions.
The Gemara explains that the difference is whether the funds can be used לכתחילה (ideally) for communal offerings without additional consecration.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Collection of the half-shekel
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Collection of the half-shekel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the half-shekel is collected from the 1st of Adar, and the collection is announced on the 15th of Adar. It also discusses the use of leftover funds.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that on the 1st of Adar, announcements are made about the half-shekel collection.
The Mishnah adds that on the 15th of Adar, the actual collection of the half-shekel begins.
The Mishnah raises the question of what is done with leftover funds from the half-shekel collection.

items.text: Gemara's question on the timing of the collection
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the timing of the collection
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the collection is announced on the 15th of Adar and not earlier. It explores the reasoning behind the date.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the collection is announced specifically on the fifteenth of Adar and not from the beginning of the month.

items.text: First answer: To allow time for the collection
items.text_en: First answer: To allow time for the collection
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the announcement is made on the 15th to give people time to prepare their donations before the collection begins on the 1st of Nisan.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers that the announcement on the 15th is to allow people time to prepare their donations before the collection begins on the 1st of Nisan.

items.text: Discussion on leftover funds
items.text_en: Discussion on leftover funds
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the use of leftover half-shekel funds, citing a baraita that they are used for the purchase of animals for the daily offerings.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that leftover half-shekel funds are used for purchasing animals for the daily offerings.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Disposal of leftover shekel funds
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Disposal of leftover shekel funds
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that leftover funds from the Temple treasury chamber (שירי הלשכה) are used for communal burnt offerings (עולות ציבור). It details that the funds are allocated for purchasing animals for the daily and additional offerings, and any surplus is used for other communal needs.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking what is done with leftover funds from the Temple treasury chamber and answers that they are used for communal burnt offerings.

items.text: Gemara's question: Are leftover funds sanctified?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Are leftover funds sanctified?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the leftover funds retain their sanctity or become non-sacred. It explores the possibility that the funds are redeemed onto animals, allowing the coins to be used for non-sacred purposes.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that leftover funds from the chamber (שירי הלשכה) are used for public needs.
The Gemara questions whether the leftover funds retain their sanctity or become non-sacred, exploring the possibility that they are redeemed onto animals.

items.text: First answer: Funds are redeemed onto animals
items.text_en: First answer: Funds are redeemed onto animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the leftover funds are redeemed onto animals designated for offerings. The coins then become non-sacred and can be used for other purposes, while the animals are offered as communal burnt offerings.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers that the leftover funds are redeemed onto animals designated for offerings, allowing the coins to become non-sacred and the animals to be offered as communal burnt offerings.

items.text: Objection: Does redemption apply to leftover funds?
items.text_en: Objection: Does redemption apply to leftover funds?
items.desc_en: An objection is raised: leftover funds are not like dedicated funds that can be redeemed, as they are already designated for communal offerings. The Gemara defends Rabbi Yochanan's position by explaining that the redemption is a rabbinic enactment to prevent misuse.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita: leftover funds (שירי הלשכה) are not subject to redemption, as they are already designated for communal offerings.
The Gemara defends Rabbi Yochanan by explaining that the redemption of leftover funds is only a rabbinic enactment (מעלה בעלמא) to prevent misuse, not a true redemption.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Surplus shekels and their use
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Surplus shekels and their use
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that surplus shekels from the temple treasury are used for the purchase of communal offerings. It specifies that the money is allocated for the daily offerings and additional offerings, with any leftover going to the maintenance of the Temple.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that surplus shekels from the temple treasury are used for communal offerings and temple maintenance.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's allocation of surplus shekels, asking whether the surplus is used for the same type of offering or for general Temple needs. It raises a contradiction from a baraita that seems to imply a different rule.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'surplus shekels' and how the surplus is used.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that seems to state a different rule for the surplus shekels.
The Gemara cites a baraita that supports the Mishnah's ruling, implying the contradiction is resolved.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion on surplus allocation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion on surplus allocation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda argues that the surplus shekels are specifically used for the purchase of the daily offerings, not for general Temple maintenance. The Gemara explains his reasoning based on a verse and a logical deduction.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that the surplus of the shekels is designated for the purchase of the daily offerings (תמידים).
The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning, deriving from a verse that the surplus is used for the daily offerings, not for general Temple maintenance.

items.text: Sages' counter-argument and resolution
items.text_en: Sages' counter-argument and resolution
items.desc_en: The Sages disagree with Rabbi Yehuda, asserting that the surplus is used for the Temple's general needs. The Gemara resolves the dispute by explaining that both opinions are based on different interpretations of the same verse, and the halakha follows the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Sages object to Rabbi Yehuda's position, asserting that the surplus of the shekel collection is allocated to the Temple's general needs.
The Gemara resolves the dispute by explaining that both opinions derive from different interpretations of the same verse, and concludes that the halakha follows the Sages.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The Omer offering from Diaspora barley
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The Omer offering from Diaspora barley
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Omer offering is brought from barley that comes from anywhere, even from the Diaspora, when the land of Israel is under foreign control. This establishes the basic rule for the Omer's source.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah establishes that the Omer offering is brought from barley that comes from anywhere, even from the Diaspora, when the land of Israel is under foreign control.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why specify Diaspora?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why specify Diaspora?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies that the Omer can come from the Diaspora, implying that normally it would come from the land of Israel. It explains that the Mishnah is addressing a situation where the land is under foreign control.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies that the Omer can come from the Diaspora, implying that normally it would come from the land of Israel, and explains that the Mishnah addresses a situation where the land is under foreign control.

items.text: Discussion of the prohibition of new grain
items.text_en: Discussion of the prohibition of new grain
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether the prohibition of eating new grain (chadash) applies to the Omer offering. It cites a baraita that the Omer permits new grain, but questions whether this applies when the Omer comes from Diaspora barley.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that the Omer offering permits the consumption of new grain (chadash).
The Gemara questions why the baraita specifies that the Omer comes from barley grown in the Land of Israel, implying that Diaspora barley might not permit new grain.
The Gemara answers that the prohibition of new grain (chadash) does not apply to grain grown outside the Land of Israel, so the Omer's permitting function is irrelevant there.

items.text: Resolution: The Omer permits new grain even from Diaspora
items.text_en: Resolution: The Omer permits new grain even from Diaspora
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Omer offering permits the new grain regardless of where the barley comes from, as the prohibition of new grain is tied to the Omer offering itself, not to the land of Israel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the Omer offering permits new grain even from the threshing floor, implying no restriction based on the grain's origin.
The Gemara concludes that the Omer permits new grain even from Diaspora, as the prohibition is tied to the offering itself, not the land.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The leftover funds
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The leftover funds
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that leftover funds from the shekel collection are used for communal burnt offerings, and the redemption of these funds must be done with the intent of the original donation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking what is done with the leftover funds of the Temple chamber (שירי הלשכה).
The Mishnah answers that the leftover funds are used to purchase communal burnt offerings (עולות).
The Mishnah adds that the redemption of these funds must be performed with the intent of the original donation (לשם אותו דבר).

items.text: Gemara's first question: What is the source?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: What is the source?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source that leftover funds are used for communal offerings, and provides an answer based on a verse from Kings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source that leftover funds from the Temple treasury are used for communal offerings.
The Gemara provides an answer based on the verse 'ויהי כצאת הכסף' (And it came to pass when the silver was brought out) from Kings, indicating that leftover funds were used for Temple repairs.

items.text: Objection and resolution: The redemption procedure
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: The redemption procedure
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the redemption must be done with specific intent, and resolves by explaining that the redemption is valid even if not explicitly stated, as long as it is for the original purpose.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that redemption requires explicit intent for the original purpose (לשם אותו דבר).
Rabbi Yochanan resolves that the redemption is valid even without explicit intent, as derived from the verse 'ויהי כצאת הכסף' (and it was when the silver came out).

items.text: Opening Mishnah and initial question
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and initial question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the high priest would place the incense on the fire before the blood of the bull. The Gemara questions this order based on a baraita that seems to imply the blood comes first.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the high priest places the incense on the fire before the blood of the bull.
The Gemara questions the Mishnah's order based on a baraita that seems to imply the blood comes first.

items.text: First answer: distinction between bull and goat
items.text_en: First answer: distinction between bull and goat
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the baraita refers to the blood of the goat, not the bull. The Mishnah's order applies to the bull's blood, while the baraita discusses the goat's blood, which is placed after the incense.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the baraita refers to the blood of the goat, not the bull, distinguishing the order of application.

items.text: Objection and resolution
items.text_en: Objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita explicitly mentions the bull's blood. It resolves by explaining that the baraita lists the order of the blood applications for the bull and goat together, but the incense is placed before both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita explicitly mentions the bull's blood, implying the incense is placed after the blood applications.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita lists the order of the blood applications for the bull and goat together, but the incense is placed before both.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that if one finds an animal designated as a sacrifice, it may be redeemed with its mother's firstborn status, and the offspring of a firstborn is treated similarly.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one finds an animal designated as a sacrifice, it may be redeemed with its mother's firstborn status, and the offspring of a firstborn is treated similarly.

items.text: Gemara's question on the mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mishnah's ruling, asking how one can redeem a found animal with its mother's firstborn status, given that the animal itself is already consecrated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can redeem a found animal with its mother's firstborn status, given that the animal itself is already consecrated.

items.text: Rabbi Yose's explanation and the Sages' dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose's explanation and the Sages' dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yose explains that the mishnah refers to redeeming the value of the animal, not the animal itself, while the Sages argue that the redemption applies to the animal's body.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yose asserts that the mishnah deals with redeeming the value of an animal set aside for a purpose, not the animal's body itself.
The Sages dispute Rabbi Yose and argue that the mishnah refers to redeeming the animal's body to permit slaughter.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may redeem a firstborn donkey with a lamb from the flock, whether the lamb is large or small, but not with a lamb that is treifah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a firstborn donkey may be redeemed with a lamb, whether large or small, but not with a lamb that is טריפה (ritually unfit).

items.text: Gemara's question on the source
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the source
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what biblical source permits redeeming a firstborn donkey with a lamb, and answers that it is derived from the verse 'and every firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb' (Exodus 13:13).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what biblical source permits redeeming a firstborn donkey with a lamb.
The Gemara answers that it is derived from the verse 'and every firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb' (Exodus 13:13).

items.text: Clarification of the lamb's status
items.text_en: Clarification of the lamb's status
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the lamb used for redemption must be a sheep, not a goat, and that it must be a year-old animal, as derived from the word 'seh' in the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the lamb for redemption must be a sheep (שה) and a year-old animal (בן שנתו), as derived from the verse.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Redeeming impure second tithe
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Redeeming impure second tithe
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if second tithe produce becomes impure, it may be redeemed even in its current state, unlike pure produce which must be brought to Jerusalem. This establishes the basic halakha for impure second tithe.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that impure second tithe produce may be redeemed even in Jerusalem, unlike pure produce which must be brought there.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's allowance to redeem impure second tithe in Jerusalem, asking why it is permitted when pure second tithe cannot be redeemed there. It seeks to understand the reasoning behind the distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah permits redeeming impure second tithe in Jerusalem, given that pure second tithe cannot be redeemed there.

items.text: First answer: Impure produce cannot be eaten
items.text_en: First answer: Impure produce cannot be eaten
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that impure second tithe cannot be eaten in Jerusalem, so it is treated like produce outside Jerusalem and may be redeemed. This distinguishes it from pure produce which can be eaten there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that impure second tithe cannot be eaten in Jerusalem, so it is treated like produce outside Jerusalem and may be redeemed.

A baraita is cited to support the answer, stating that second tithe that became impure may be redeemed and eaten in Jerusalem only if it was impure from the start, but if it became impure in Jerusalem it is not redeemed.
The Gemara concludes that impure second tithe is treated like בשר תאוה (ordinary meat), which may be redeemed and eaten anywhere, thus resolving the difficulty.

items.text: Objection and second answer: Comparison to pure produce
items.text_en: Objection and second answer: Comparison to pure produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that pure produce also cannot be redeemed in Jerusalem, and offers a second answer: the Mishnah refers to a case where the produce became impure after being set aside, and the redemption is permitted because it is like redeeming a firstborn animal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that pure produce (טהור) also cannot be redeemed in Jerusalem, so the Mishnah's allowance for impure produce is not unique.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah deals with a case where the produce became impure after being set aside for the Temple treasury.
The Gemara supports the answer by comparing the redemption of impure Temple produce to the redemption of a firstborn animal (בכור), which is permitted even in Jerusalem.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Coins found in Jerusalem
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Coins found in Jerusalem
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that coins found in Jerusalem are presumed to be secular unless found on the Temple Mount or in the treasury chambers, where they are considered consecrated. This sets up the basic rule for determining the status of found coins.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that coins found in Jerusalem are presumed to be secular (חולין) unless found on the Temple Mount or in the treasury chambers, where they are considered consecrated (קודש).

items.text: Gemara's first question: Why distinguish between Temple Mount and elsewhere?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Why distinguish between Temple Mount and elsewhere?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's distinction, asking why coins found on the Temple Mount are considered consecrated while those found elsewhere in Jerusalem are secular. It suggests that perhaps the majority of coins in Jerusalem are consecrated, but the Mishnah follows a different principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah distinguishes between the Temple Mount and elsewhere in Jerusalem regarding the status of found coins.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the Mishnah's ruling is based on the principle of רוב (majority), but the Gemara questions whether the majority of coins in Jerusalem are consecrated.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the majority of coins in Jerusalem are consecrated, which would undermine the Mishnah's distinction.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah follows the principle of רוב (majority) but applies it differently on the Temple Mount versus elsewhere.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's answer: Following the majority of the area
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's answer: Following the majority of the area
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the rule follows the majority of coins typically found in each area: on the Temple Mount, most coins are consecrated, while elsewhere in Jerusalem, most are secular. This resolves the Mishnah's distinction.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan introduces the principle that the halachic status of coins follows the majority of coins typically found in each area.

items.text: Objection and clarification: The case of the treasury chambers
items.text_en: Objection and clarification: The case of the treasury chambers
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: if the rule is based on majority, why does the Mishnah specify that coins found in the treasury chambers are consecrated? It clarifies that the treasury chambers are a special case where all coins are consecrated, so the majority principle still holds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the rule is based on רוב (majority), why does the Mishnah specify that coins found in the treasury chambers (לשכות) are consecrated, implying a special rule?
The Gemara answers: the treasury chambers are a special case where all coins are consecrated (קודש), so the majority principle still holds for other locations.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The half-shekel and the Temple treasury
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The half-shekel and the Temple treasury
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the half-shekel is collected from all Israelites, and the funds are used for communal offerings. It also discusses the case of one who has not yet donated and wishes to use Temple funds.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the half-shekel is collected from all Israelites and the funds are used for communal offerings, including the case of one who has not yet donated and wishes to use Temple funds.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Can one use Temple funds without donating?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Can one use Temple funds without donating?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a person who has not yet given his half-shekel may take from the Temple treasury to fulfill his obligation, and explores the logic behind the Mishnah's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a person who has not yet donated his half-shekel may take from the Temple treasury (תרומת הלשכה) to fulfill his obligation, or not.

The Gemara answers that the verse 'כל העובר על הפקודים' (everyone who passes the count) implies that one may take from the treasury even without prior donation, because the donation is collected from the public fund.
The Gemara concludes that one may take from the treasury to fulfill the obligation, based on the verse's inclusive language.

items.text: First answer: Distinction between voluntary and obligatory donations
items.text_en: First answer: Distinction between voluntary and obligatory donations
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah distinguishes between voluntary donations, which can be taken from the treasury, and obligatory ones, which cannot. This is based on a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the contradiction is resolved by distinguishing voluntary donations from obligatory ones.
The Gemara cites a verse to support the distinction between voluntary and obligatory donations.

items.text: Objection: Stolen money for the half-shekel
items.text_en: Objection: Stolen money for the half-shekel
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: if one stole money and used it for the half-shekel donation, is the donation valid? This leads to a discussion of the principle of 'mitzvah haba'ah ba'averah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: if one stole money and used it for the half-shekel donation, is the donation valid? This is framed as a question about the applicability of the principle of 'mitzvah haba'ah ba'averah'.

items.text: Resolution: The status of stolen money in Temple donations
items.text_en: Resolution: The status of stolen money in Temple donations
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by stating that stolen money cannot be used for the half-shekel, as it is not considered the donor's property. This is supported by a baraita.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution: stolen money invalid for half-shekel
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution: stolen money invalid for half-shekel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that stolen money cannot be used for the half-shekel (מחצית השקל), because it is not the property of the donor, citing the principle that a גזלן (robber) has no ownership.

A supporting baraita is cited, which explicitly rules that if a person steals and attempts to consecrate the stolen item, it is not consecrated (אינו קדוש), thereby applying the same logic to the half-shekel.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Coins found in Jerusalem
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Coins found in Jerusalem
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that coins found in Jerusalem during the festival season are considered secular, but those found during the rest of the year are considered consecrated, because people would bring consecrated coins to the Temple and may have dropped them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the rule for coins found in Jerusalem: during the festival season they are secular, during the rest of the year they are consecrated.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why the distinction?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why the distinction?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why coins found during the festival are considered secular, while those found during the rest of the year are considered consecrated. It suggests that perhaps the majority of coins in Jerusalem at any time are consecrated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why coins found during the festival are treated as secular while those found the rest of the year are treated as consecrated, suggesting that perhaps the majority of coins in Jerusalem at any time are consecrated.
Rabbi Yochanan begins his answer to the Gemara's question.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's answer: Following the majority of the area
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's answer: Following the majority of the area
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that during the festival, the majority of coins in Jerusalem are secular because people come from outside and bring secular coins, while during the rest of the year, the majority are consecrated because only locals are present.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers that during the festival the majority of coins in Jerusalem are secular (חולין) because visitors bring secular coins, while the rest of the year the majority are consecrated (הקדש) due to the local population.

items.text: Objection and resolution: Coins found near the Temple
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: Coins found near the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that coins found near the Temple might always be consecrated, but resolves that the Mishnah's rule applies to coins found anywhere in Jerusalem, and the principle of following the majority of the area applies.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects that coins found near the Temple might always be consecrated (הקדש), challenging the Mishnah's rule.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's rule applies to coins found anywhere in Jerusalem, and the principle of following the majority of the area (רוב) applies, so the coins are not automatically consecrated.

items.text: Mishnah: Coins found in the Temple treasury
items.text_en: Mishnah: Coins found in the Temple treasury
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that coins found in the Temple treasury, or in Jerusalem during a festival, are considered consecrated (for the Temple). Coins found elsewhere in Jerusalem are secular.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that coins found in the Temple Mount area or in Jerusalem during a festival are consecrated (קודש), while those found elsewhere in Jerusalem are secular (חולין).

items.text: Gemara's question: Why are coins found in Jerusalem during a festival consecrated?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why are coins found in Jerusalem during a festival consecrated?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why coins found in Jerusalem during a festival are considered consecrated, since people might bring secular coins for their own needs. It suggests that the Mishnah refers to coins found near the Temple treasury, which are assumed to be from the half-shekel collection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why coins found in Jerusalem during a festival are considered consecrated, given that people might bring secular coins for their own needs.
The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah refers to coins found near the Temple treasury, which are assumed to be from the half-shekel collection.

items.text: Supporting verse and conclusion
items.text_en: Supporting verse and conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse to support the distinction between festival and non-festival times, and concludes that the Mishnah's ruling is based on the assumption that people bring consecrated coins to the Temple during festivals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'ולא יראה' (and he shall not appear empty-handed) to support the distinction between festival and non-festival times.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's ruling is based on the assumption that people bring consecrated coins to the Temple during festivals.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Lost or stolen coins
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Lost or stolen coins
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where someone sets aside coins for the half-shekel tax and they are lost or stolen. If the owner then designates other coins and later the original coins are found, the original coins and the replacement coins both belong to the Temple treasury, but the owner is credited only once.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the case: one who sets aside his half-shekel and it is lost or stolen, then designates another, and later the original is found — both coins belong to the Temple treasury, and the owner is credited only once.

items.text: Gemara's question: Does the owner owe another half-shekel?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Does the owner owe another half-shekel?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the owner is obligated to pay another half-shekel if the original coins were lost before being given to the treasury. It explores the principle that the Temple treasury acquires the coins at the moment of designation, but the owner may still be liable if the coins were not actually delivered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the owner is obligated to pay another half-shekel if the designated coins were lost before delivery, based on the principle that the Temple treasury acquires the coins at designation but the owner remains liable for their safekeeping.
The Gemara answers that according to Rabbi Yochanan, the owner is not liable for the loss because the Temple treasury already acquired the coins at the moment of designation.
The Gemara concludes that according to Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, the owner remains liable for the coins until they are actually delivered to the treasury.

items.text: First answer: Designation as acquisition
items.text_en: First answer: Designation as acquisition
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that once a person designates coins for the half-shekel, the Temple treasury acquires them immediately, so the owner is not liable for loss. However, this is challenged because the Mishnah implies the owner must replace lost coins.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers that once a person designates coins for the half-shekel, the Temple treasury acquires them immediately, so the owner is not liable for loss.
The Gemara objects that if acquisition occurs immediately, the Mishnah's implication that the owner must replace lost coins would be contradicted.

items.text: Second answer: Liability until delivery
items.text_en: Second answer: Liability until delivery
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the owner remains responsible for the coins until they are actually handed over to the Temple treasury. The designation alone does not transfer ownership; the coins must be physically delivered to the treasury chamber.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves that the owner remains liable for the coins until they physically reach the Temple treasurer (גזבר), not merely upon designation.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The rule of leftover shekalim
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The rule of leftover shekalim
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that leftover funds from the collection of shekalim are used for the purchase of communal offerings, and any surplus after the year's needs is set aside for the next year.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking what was done with leftover funds from the shekel collection chamber, and answers that they were used for communal offerings, with any surplus set aside for the next year.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Can leftover funds be used for other purposes?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Can leftover funds be used for other purposes?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the leftover shekalim can be used for other communal needs, such as the purchase of wine or oil for offerings, or if they are restricted to the specific purpose of the original collection.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the topic of leftover funds in the Temple chamber (שירי הלשכה) and asks what was done with them.
The Gemara questions the purpose of the leftover shekalim, asking whether they are designated for specific uses or can be redirected.
The Gemara presents the alternative possibility that the leftover funds may not be usable for other purposes.

items.text: First answer: They are used for the same type of offering
items.text_en: First answer: They are used for the same type of offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the leftover funds are used for the same type of offering for which the original shekalim were collected, meaning they are dedicated to communal sacrifices and cannot be diverted to other purposes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that leftover funds from the chamber (שירי הלשכה) are used for burnt offerings (עולות), establishing that leftover shekalim are dedicated to communal sacrifices.

items.text: Objection: The case of leftover wine and oil
items.text_en: Objection: The case of leftover wine and oil
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection based on a baraita that discusses leftover wine and oil from offerings, suggesting that they may be used for other purposes, which contradicts the previous answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about leftover wine and oil, implying they may be used for libations, contradicting the prior answer.

items.text: Resolution: Distinction between shekalim and other funds
items.text_en: Resolution: Distinction between shekalim and other funds
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing between the leftover shekalim, which are designated for communal offerings, and leftover wine or oil, which are not subject to the same restriction because they are not from the shekel collection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between leftover shekalim, which are designated for communal offerings, and leftover wine or oil, which are not from the shekel collection and thus not subject to the same restriction.

items.text: Surplus of shekel funds for communal offerings
items.text_en: Surplus of shekel funds for communal offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that surplus funds from the shekel collection for communal offerings are allocated to the same purpose. The Gemara questions whether this applies to all surpluses or only to those not designated for a specific item.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that surplus funds from the shekel collection for communal offerings are allocated to the same purpose, and the Gemara begins to question whether this applies to all surpluses or only to those not designated for a specific item.
The Gemara asks what the purpose of the surplus allocation is, implying a need for clarification.

items.text: Surplus of funds for the red heifer
items.text_en: Surplus of funds for the red heifer
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether surplus funds designated for the red heifer are used for the same purpose or for other communal needs. It cites a baraita that indicates the surplus is used for other communal offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether surplus funds designated for the red heifer (פרה אדומה) are used for the same purpose or for other communal needs.
A baraita is cited that explicitly states the surplus of the red heifer funds is used for other communal needs (לצורכי ציבור).
The Gemara clarifies that 'communal needs' (לצורכי ציבור) refers to other offerings for the community, resolving the question.

items.text: Surplus of funds for the goat of Azazel
items.text_en: Surplus of funds for the goat of Azazel
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines whether surplus funds set aside for the goat of Azazel are used for the same purpose or for other communal needs. It concludes that the surplus is used for other communal offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by asking what is done with the surplus of funds designated for the goat of Azazel (שעיר המשתלח).
A baraita is cited to provide the ruling: the surplus of the goat of Azazel is used for other communal needs (לצורכי ציבור).
The Gemara concludes that the surplus is indeed allocated for communal purposes, resolving the inquiry.

items.text: Distinction between designated and undesignated surpluses
items.text_en: Distinction between designated and undesignated surpluses
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the rule for surplus funds depends on whether the funds were designated for a specific item or for a general category. Designated surpluses go to other communal needs, while undesignated surpluses remain for the same purpose.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the rule for surplus funds depends on whether the funds were designated for a specific item or for a general category.
The Gemara explains that designated surpluses go to other communal needs, while undesignated surpluses remain for the same purpose.
The Gemara further clarifies the distinction between designated and undesignated surpluses.
